Delay differential equations through rxstan

Source: vignettes/rxstan-dde.Rmd
rxstan-dde.Rmd

Delay differential equations: a Stan limitation

Stan has no DDE solver. Not a slow one – none. There is no ode_* function that accepts a lagged state, and you cannot write one in the Stan language, because the solution has to be interpolated at t−τt - \tau while it is still being computed.

However, rxode2 has delay(), and it propagates sensitivities through the delay correctly. Because nlmixr2bayes links Stan to a likelihood rather than translating a model into the Stan language, that limitation never reaches Stan: whatever rxode2 can solve, Stan can sample.

So a DDE is reachable both ways nlmixr2bayes offers, and this vignette walks the same example through each:

  1. Automatically – nlmixr2(model, data, est = "nuts") on an ordinary nlmixr2 model containing delay(). No Stan code, and nothing special to configure.
  2. Hand-coded – register the DDE as a solver backend with rxsRegister() and call it from a Stan program you wrote yourself (see vignette("rxstan-handcoded", "nlmixr2bayes") for the general pattern), which is also the level at which you can inspect the delayed sensitivities directly.

A delayed indirect response

Turnover with delayed feedback: the loss term depends on the response one delay ago rather than now.

dRdt=kin−koutR(t−τ),R(s)=1fors≤0\frac{dR}{dt} = k_{in} - k_{out}\,R(t - \tau), \qquad R(s) = 1 \ \text{for}\ s \le 0

R(0) <- 1 does double duty: it is the initial condition and the pre-history, so delay(R, tau) returns 1 whenever t−τ≤0t - \tau \le 0. Everything is parameterized on the log scale (lkin, lkout, ltau), which is the scale Stan samples on and keeps all three positive without a constraint.

Part 1: the automatic path

Written as an nlmixr2 model with priors, the delay is just another line – there is nothing DDE-specific in the ini({}) block.

The delay itself is fix()ed here, and that is a current limitation rather than a modelling choice: nlmixr2est’s theta-sensitivity model returns an identically zero derivative for a parameter that reaches the model only as a delay() lag (nlmixr2est#1122). Stan is then told the target is flat in ltau when it is in fact steep, and the fit does not sample: every iteration saturates max_treedepth and the chain does not mix (Rhat 2.2 in the case that prompted the issue). est = "nuts" warns when a model estimates such a parameter. Part 2 below estimates the delay with correct sensitivities, through rxsRegister(), which is the path to use for that today.

library(nlmixr2)
library(nlmixr2bayes)

ddeMod <- function() {
  ini({
    lkin <- c(log(0.05), log(0.7), log(10))
    lkout <- c(log(0.02), log(0.4), log(5))
    ltau <- fix(log(1.5))
    add.sd <- c(0, 0.3)
    eta.kin ~ 0.05
    prior(lkin) ~ dnorm(log(0.7), 0.5)
    prior(lkout) ~ dnorm(log(0.4), 0.5)
    prior(add.sd) ~ dcauchy(0, 1)
  })
  model({
    kin <- exp(lkin + eta.kin)
    kout <- exp(lkout)
    tau <- exp(ltau)
    R(0) <- 1
    d/dt(R) <- kin - kout * delay(R, tau)
    R ~ add(add.sd)
  })
}

Twelve subjects, simulated from the model itself so there is a known truth to recover:

set.seed(42)
tmsAuto <- seq(0.5, 12, by = 1)
evAuto <- rxode2::et(tmsAuto)
evAuto <- rxode2::et(evAuto, id = 1:12)

simAuto := rxode2::rxSolve(ddeMod, evAuto, returnType = "data.frame")
datAuto <- as.data.frame(evAuto)
names(datAuto) <- tolower(names(datAuto))
datAuto$dv <- simAuto$sim
head(datAuto, 3)
#>   id time evid       dv
#> 1  1  0.5    0 1.518050
#> 2  1  1.5    0 1.290215
#> 3  1  2.5    0 1.630253

And that is the whole fit – an ordinary est = "nuts" call, at Stan’s default max_treedepth. := is nlmixr2save’s caching assignment, so it runs once and is reloaded on later builds:

fitAuto := nlmixr2est::nlmixr2(ddeMod, datAuto, est = "nuts",
                               control = nutsControl(seed = 42, chains = 2,
                                                     iter = 1000))
print(fitAuto)

The posterior sits on the simulating values:

truthAuto <- c(lkin = log(0.7), lkout = log(0.4), add.sd = 0.3)
cbind(truth = truthAuto,
      posterior = fitAuto$posteriorSummary[names(truthAuto), "mean"],
      `2.5%` = fitAuto$posteriorSummary[names(truthAuto), "2.5%"],
      `97.5%` = fitAuto$posteriorSummary[names(truthAuto), "97.5%"])
#>             truth  posterior       2.5%      97.5%
#> lkin   -0.3566749 -0.4873861 -0.6933766 -0.2839434
#> lkout  -0.9162907 -0.9343854 -1.1119005 -0.7434201
#> add.sd  0.3000000  0.3398187  0.3005292  0.3846784

Two practical notes, both of them about the solver rather than about Stan:

  • rxode2 detects the delay and picks a dense-output method itself, the same way it does under est = "focei" or est = "saem"; nothing in stanControl() mentions DDEs.
  • A DDE solve is expensive, and HMC asks for one per gradient, so expect DDE fits to be slower per draw than the equivalent ODE fit. With the lag fix()ed this one needs no more than Stan’s default tree depth: about 31 leapfrog steps per iteration, no divergences, and half a minute of sampling per chain.
  • The rate parameters are bounded in ini({}). A delay solve’s cost grows like 1/lag, and an unbounded proposal at an absurd rate or lag can leave a single solve running with its dense history growing without bound – rxControl(maxsteps=) and hmin do not stop it. est = "nuts" rejects a proposal whose eta is beyond 100 ini() omega standard deviations before ever calling the solver, but bounding the structural parameters of a DDE is worth doing too.

Part 2: the bridge view

The rest of this vignette works the same equation one level lower, through rxsRegister(). That is the level you want when you are writing the Stan program yourself – and it is also the most direct way to see the delayed sensitivities, which the automatic path keeps inside the likelihood.

library(nlmixr2bayes)

dde <- "
kin  <- exp(lkin)
kout <- exp(lkout)
tau  <- exp(ltau)
R(0) <- 1
d/dt(R) <- kin - kout * delay(R, tau)
"

The same equation as a bare rxode2 model, with no residual model or priors – the Stan program supplies those:

Register the DDE model

Register it the same way as any other model. All three parameters are differentiated, including the delay:

tms <- seq(0.25, 25, by = 0.25)
h <- rxsRegister(dde, events = rxode2::et(tms),
                 sens = c("lkin", "lkout", "ltau"), output = "R",
                 atol = 1e-10, rtol = 1e-10, method = "dop853")
#> [====|====|====|====|====|====|====|====|====|====] 0:00:00
#> [====|====|====|====|====|====|====|====|====|====] 0:00:00
h
#> <rxstan handle 1>
#>   parameters (3): lkin, lkout, ltau
#>   states     (1): R
#>   rows       : 100 obs -> 100 outputs

method = "dop853" rather than the default liblsoda: the delay machinery needs a solver that keeps a dense history to interpolate from.

The handle prints the layout Stan will see – three parameters in, one state out, one row per requested time. That 100 obs -> 100 outputs line is what the Stan program’s vector[nObs] has to match.

Solve and inspect the sensitivities

rxsSolve() calls the same C entry point the Stan program does, so it is the direct way to see what crosses the bridge:

truth <- c(kin = 0.7, kout = 0.4, tau = 1.5)
p <- log(unname(truth))
res <- rxsSolve(h, p)
head(res, 3)
#>       [,1]  [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,] 1.075 0.175 -0.1    0
#> [2,] 1.150 0.350 -0.2    0
#> [3,] 1.225 0.525 -0.3    0

Column 1 is RR; the rest are ∂R/∂(ℓkin,ℓkout,ℓτ)\partial R/\partial(\ell k_{in}, \ell k_{out}, \ell\tau). The fourth column is exactly zero in those first rows, and that is correct rather than suspicious: before the first delay has elapsed the solution has not yet seen the lagged term, so it does not depend on τ\tau at all. It becomes non-zero once t>τt > \tau:

range(res[tms <= truth[["tau"]], 4])   # before the first delay
#> [1] 0 0
range(res[tms >  truth[["tau"]], 4])   # after it
#> [1] -0.08528119  0.38250000

Checking it without trusting finite differences

Before the first delay has elapsed there is a closed form, and it makes a much better test than differencing the solver against itself.

While t≤τt \le \tau the lagged term is still the constant pre-history, so the equation collapses to R′=kin−koutR' = k_{in} - k_{out}, giving R=1+(kin−kout)tR = 1 + (k_{in} - k_{out})t. On the log scale the sensitivities are then exactly kintk_{in}t and −koutt-k_{out}t:

early <- which(tms <= truth[["tau"]])
data.frame(t        = tms[early],
           dlkin    = res[early, 2],
           exact    = truth[["kin"]] * tms[early],
           dlkout   = res[early, 3],
           exact2   = -truth[["kout"]] * tms[early])
#>      t dlkin exact dlkout exact2
#> 1 0.25 0.175 0.175   -0.1   -0.1
#> 2 0.50 0.350 0.350   -0.2   -0.2
#> 3 0.75 0.525 0.525   -0.3   -0.3
#> 4 1.00 0.700 0.700   -0.4   -0.4
#> 5 1.25 0.875 0.875   -0.5   -0.5
#> 6 1.50 1.050 1.050   -0.6   -0.6

An exact match (to solver tolerances) verifies that the delay itself and its derivatives are handled correctly:

max(abs(res[early, 2] - truth[["kin"]] * tms[early]))
#> [1] 3.330669e-16
max(abs(res[early, 3] + truth[["kout"]] * tms[early]))
#> [1] 3.330669e-16

Past the first delay interval there is no closed form left, so the fallback there is central differences of whole solves – which is what rxsCheckGradient() does once the model is compiled into Stan.

Using the DDE in a hand-coded Stan program

Once registered, use it in Stan exactly as you would an ODE:

ddeStan <- "
functions {
  vector rx_solve(int handle, vector p);
}
data {
  int<lower=1> nObs;
  int<lower=1> handle;
  vector[nObs] rObs;
}
parameters {
  real lkin;
  real lkout;
  real ltau;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  vector[3] p = [lkin, lkout, ltau]';
  vector[nObs] r = rx_solve(handle, p);

  lkin ~ normal(0, 1);
  lkout ~ normal(-1, 1);
  ltau ~ normal(0, 1);
  sigma ~ exponential(1);

  rObs ~ normal(r, sigma);
}
"

Nothing in it mentions a delay: from Stan’s side rx_solve() is just a function with known partials. rstan::stanc() confirms it is a valid program – allow_undefined is what lets rx_solve() stay undeclared until the bridge supplies it at link time:

sc <- rstan::stanc(model_code = ddeStan, model_name = "dde",
                   allow_undefined = TRUE)
sc$status
#> [1] TRUE

Compiling and fitting it is then the ordinary pattern from vignette("rxstan-handcoded", "nlmixr2bayes") – write ddeStan to a .stan file, rxsStanModel() it, and rstan::sampling() with list(nObs = length(rObs), handle = h, rObs = rObs):

f <- tempfile(fileext = ".stan")
writeLines(ddeStan, f)
sm <- rxsStanModel(f, modelName = "dde")
fit := rstan::sampling(sm, data = list(nObs = length(rObs), handle = h,
                                       rObs = rObs),
                       chains = 2, iter = 1000)

The bridge compiles the rxode2 model with the forward-sensitivity DDE system augmented, solves it, and supplies both the solution and its derivatives to Stan’s reverse-mode autodiff. No DDE solver in Stan; no finite differencing; exact sensitivities.

Key points

  • DDEs require dense output: Use method = "dop853" or another dense solver, and set dense = TRUE in rxControl().
  • The delay itself is a parameter: You can estimate the lag time τ\tau, and its gradient flows through the sensitivity equations correctly.
  • Pre-history must be constant: The initial condition R(0) <- 1 defines both the condition at t=0t=0 and the pre-history for t<0t < 0. It must be a constant (not a function of time or parameters).
  • The fast path is automatic: rxstan detects DDEs and enables the fast path when safe; rxsFastAvailable() reports whether this handle got it (a modelled alag()/f()/dur()/rate() with dose rows is the case that refuses it):
rxsFastAvailable(h)
#> [1] TRUE

Release the handle when you are done with it:

rxsRelease(h)
